Females of White-eye bream attain a maximum total length of 35 cm [Li = 35 cm], a size that distinguishes them as one of the larger-bodied cyprinids within their native range. The species exhibits a pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with females consistently reaching larger ultimate dimensions than males, a pattern commonly linked to fecundity selection in iteroparous freshwater teleosts. The relationship between length and mass in this species has been estimated using a power-law growth equation, from which the ultimate wet weight can be derived. Based on this allometric relationship, a female at her asymptotic length reaches a body mass of 584 grams [Wwi = 584 grams], a value that reflects the substantial somatic investment required to support the production of large egg masses typical of mid-sized cyprinids. This adult body mass places the white-eye bream at an intermediate position within its genus, somewhat smaller than the closely related Ballerus ballerus but considerably larger than many riverine leuciscids found in sympatry. Field collections from the Volga and Don river systems consistently confirm this maximum size, with the largest individuals captured in slow-flowing sections of larger rivers.

Puberty is initiated at a total length of 19 cm [Lp = 19 cm], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 88 grams [Wwp = approximately 88 grams] based on the species-specific length-weight conversion. This size at sexual maturation is notably modest relative to the species ultimate length, suggesting that individuals allocate resources to gonadal development relatively early in their growth trajectory, a life-history strategy conducive to high fecundity over a protracted reproductive lifespan. The attainment of puberty is not strictly size-dependent; it also appears to be influenced by local thermal regimes and food availability, with fish in productive floodplain habitats maturing at slightly smaller sizes than those in oligotrophic reservoirs. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from wild-caught juveniles confirms that the transition to reproductive competence begins as the fish approach this total length, with the first signs of vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis becoming evident. The body mass at this developmental milestone is a fraction of the ultimate adult weight, emphasizing the prolonged period of somatic growth that follows the onset of reproductive capability.

At hatching, the newly emerged prolarvae possess a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.002 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.002 grams], an exceedingly small initial mass that is typical of cyprinids producing pelagic eggs of modest diameter. This neonatal mass is derived from an estimated egg diameter of 1.575 millimeters, consistent with the oocyte sizes recorded in related bramids, and represents the entirety of the endogenous yolk reserves that must sustain the larva until the onset of exogenous feeding. The tiny size of the yolk-sac larva makes it highly vulnerable to starvation and predation during the initial days post-eclosion, a critical bottleneck in the early life history of this species. After the mouth opens and the yolk-sac is largely resorbed, the first-feeding larva must capture suitable planktonic prey within a narrow time window or face irreversible starvation, commonly referred to as the point of no return. This extreme dependence on early feeding success is a key determinant of year-class strength in white-eye bream populations, linking recruitment variability directly to the timing and abundance of spring zooplankton blooms in its riverine habitats.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of white-eye bream has been quantified through observations of spawning frequency and fecundity. Females exhibit a high fecundity per reproductive event, producing approximately 274 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 274 eggs per spawning event] during their peak reproductive season. This per-event fecundity is complemented by a spawning frequency of roughly one event per day [F_R_i = roughly one event per day] under optimal thermal conditions, indicating a capacity for nearly daily gamete release over the spawning period. Such a combination of high per-clutch output and extreme spawning frequency is unusual among temperate cyprinids and suggests that the white-eye bream has evolved a strategy of continuous, batch spawning to exploit brief windows of favorable planktonic conditions for larval survival. The rate of egg production at this temperature is among the highest recorded for any leuciscid of comparable body size, highlighting the energetic demands imposed on reproductively active females.

The maximum lifespan of white-eye bream in natural populations reaches approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] at a mean annual water temperature of 12 °C, a longevity that is considerable for a cyprinid of its body size and reproductive strat at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]egy. This extended lifespan, equivalent to roughly 5475 days, allows for repeated spawning events over many seasons, contributing to the species demographic resilience in variable riverine environments. Old individuals, particularly females, continue to reproduce at advanced ages, although fecundity may decline slightly due to the onset of reproductive senescence in the oldest age classes. Mark-recapture studies conducted in the middle reaches of the Danube have confirmed that individuals exceeding 12 years of age remain in good somatic condition, with growth increments slowing substantially after the tenth year. The species iteroparous life cycle, combined with a moderate growth rate and delayed senescence, aligns well with the bet-hedging strategy typical of cyprinids inhabiting unpredictable floodplain ecosystems where recruitment success depends on sporadic environmental cues.
